content: A pterygium is a benign, whitish-pink, triangular-shaped growth of tissue that develops on the conjunctiva, the clear tissue covering the white part of the eye. It most commonly originates from the nasal side of the eye and extends toward the cornea. While it rarely grows large enough to cover the pupil, its progression varies; some pterygia grow slowly over a person’s lifetime, while others stop growing at a certain point. It can affect one or both eyes. The primary symptom of a pterygium is a painless, elevated area of whitish-pink tissue with visible blood vessels, typically located on the inner or outer edge of the cornea. The exact cause of pterygium is unknown. However, it is strongly associated with prolonged exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun. This is supported by the observation that individuals with pterygium often spend significant time outdoors. Pterygium is more common in individuals aged 20 to 40 who live in sunny, dry climates. Chronic dry eye is also thought to contribute to its development. Risk factors include exposure to environments that are sunny, dusty, sandy, or windy. Occupations such as farming and fishing, as well as living near the equator, increase the likelihood of developing pterygium. Some studies suggest a higher prevalence in men, possibly due to greater UV light exposure. Pterygium is rarely seen in children. Diagnosis of pterygium is typically made through a physical examination of the eyes and eyelids. Special diagnostic tests are usually unnecessary. Urgent medical care is not typically required for pterygium. However, if the growth begins to impair vision, it is important to consult an ophthalmologist for treatment. Individuals with pterygium should have annual eye exams to monitor the condition and address any changes before vision is affected. Those with a history of pterygium should also seek medical attention if symptoms recur. Treatment is not necessary unless the pterygium begins to obstruct vision. Lubricating eye drops can help reduce redness and alleviate chronic irritation. If the pterygium affects vision, surgical removal is recommended. Some individuals may seek surgical removal for cosmetic reasons, but this is generally not advised. Surgical removal carries a risk of recurrence, particularly in patients under 40 years of age. If the pterygium recurs after surgery or poses a threat to vision, strontium-90 (90Sr) plaque therapy may be used. This treatment involves the application of a radioactive substance that emits beta particles, which penetrate a short distance into the cornea at the surgical site. It suppresses the regrowth of blood vessels associated with pterygium recurrence. This therapy is typically performed under local anesthesia and is best done at the time of, or on the same day as, the surgical excision. Conditions with similar symptoms include pinguecula, a related but distinct conjunctival growth. To prevent pterygium, individuals in areas with strong sunlight are advised to wear protective eyewear, such as sunglasses, and hats with brims. Most pterygia do not cause significant problems and do not require treatment. If a pterygium affects vision or the cornea, surgical removal usually yields good results. However, there is a possibility of recurrence after removal.
